subtitle: Midterm Important Subjective Questions (Solved)
topics: Humanistic and Other Models of Crime

subjective.question: Define forensic psychology. Also describe its scope and main activities. Forensic psychology is the application of psychological knowledge, methods and research to issues relating to law and the legal system (Wrightsman); Bartol and Bartol describe it as research and practice relating to the legal system and the professionals who work in it. Its scope is very broad: it includes police psychology, investigative psychology and offender profiling, psychological assessment of offenders and suspects, expert testimony in court, child custody evaluations, assessment of competency and criminal responsibility, false confession research, psychological autopsies, correctional psychology and work with victims. Forensic psychologists work with police, courts, prisons and legal professionals, which is why the recommended route is to qualify first as a clinical psychologist and then specialise in forensic work.

Describe the work and functions of a police psychologist. A police psychologist works with law-enforcement agencies in several areas. (1) Selection: screening-out unsuitable applicants using psychological tests such as the MMPI and the Inwald Personality Inventory (IPI). (2) Training: helping officers develop empathy, communication and customer-service skills and an understanding of human behaviour. (3) Operational support: assisting investigations through interviewing strategies, offender profiling and psychological autopsies. (4) Counselling and stress management: helping officers cope with occupational stress and post-shooting trauma, and conducting fitness-for-duty evaluations (FFDE) of officers involved in critical incidents. (5) Organisational consultation: advising management on personnel and community-relations issues. The first police psychologist was Martin Reiser, appointed by the Los Angeles Police Department in 1968.

What is excessive force? Discuss its causes and how it can be combated at different levels. Excessive force exists when the level of force used by a police officer exceeds that which is justifiable in the situation. Bartol (1982) found that officers prone to excessive force fall into two personality groups: those with an antisocial personality pattern and those with an ineffectual personality pattern; certain PERSEREC traits also correlate with brutality and corruption. It can be combated at three levels: (1) Selection — screening-out applicants with antisocial or ineffectual traits through psychological testing; (2) Training — teaching empathy, communication, customer service and lawful use-of-force judgement; (3) Counselling and supervision — stress management, monitoring of complaint-prone officers, and fitness-for-duty evaluations after critical incidents.

Discuss the MMPI as a tool of police selection. List its validity and clinical scales. The Minnesota Multiphasic Personality Inventory (MMPI) was developed in 1940 at the University of Minnesota and contains 567 true/false items. It is widely used in screening-out unsuitable police applicants. It has 6 validity scales, which detect lying, defensiveness, random responding and exaggeration, and 10 clinical scales, in order: 1. Hs — Hypochondriasis, 2. D — Depression, 3. Hy — Hysteria, 4. Pd — Psychopathic Deviate, 5. Mf — Masculinity/Femininity, 6. Pa — Paranoia, 7. Pt — Psychasthenia, 8. Sc — Schizophrenia, 9. Ma — Hypomania, 10. Si — Social Introversion. Elevated profiles, especially on Pd and Ma, help identify applicants at risk of misconduct, impulsivity and excessive force.

What are false confessions? Describe Kassin's three types. A false confession is an admission of guilt for a crime the person did not commit — a serious problem documented in cases such as the Lindbergh kidnapping (1932), where more than 200 people confessed. Kassin (1997) classified false confessions into three types: (1) Voluntary false confessions — given without police pressure, for attention and publicity, or to protect the real offender. (2) Coerced-compliant false confessions — the suspect knows he is innocent but confesses to escape the pressure of interrogation or to gain a promised benefit. (3) Coerced-internalized false confessions — through suggestive interrogation the suspect actually comes to believe that he committed the crime.

How can forensic psychology help the police in Pakistan? Forensic psychology can assist Pakistani police in many practical ways: scientific screening-in and screening-out of recruits through psychological testing (MMPI, IPI) to reduce brutality and corruption; training officers in empathy, communication, stress management and lawful use of force so that excessive-force incidents decline; investigative support through offender profiling, interview strategies and psychological autopsies in equivocal deaths; evaluation of suspects' competency and detection of false confessions; counselling and fitness-for-duty evaluations for officers exposed to trauma; and research-based reforms of interrogation practice so that evidence becomes more reliable in court.

Describe the profile of the typical 1970s aircraft hijacker. Why is it no longer valid? During the hijacking epidemic (36 hijackings in 1968, 71 in 1969 and 69 in 1970), investigators developed a profile of the typical hijacker as a person who was unsuccessful in life, socially inadequate, held an unsteady occupation, lacked resourcefulness, felt helpless and hopeless, was suicidal, and had an unconscious desire for control. This profile is no longer valid because the motives and backgrounds of hijackers changed radically — later hijackings were committed by organised, ideologically motivated groups rather than lone, inadequate individuals, so a profile built on the earlier population produces false positives and false negatives and cannot be relied upon.

Differentiate between organized and disorganized crime scenes. An organized crime scene reflects a planned offence by a controlled, intelligent offender: the victim is often a targeted stranger, the offender brings weapons and restraints, controls the victim through conversation, commits the act away from the living area, removes the body or evidence, and leaves little forensic evidence. A disorganized crime scene reflects an impulsive, spontaneous offence: the victim is often known or encountered by chance, the attack is sudden and frenzied, the body is left at the scene in view, the weapon comes from the scene itself, and abundant physical evidence is left behind. Kocsis et al. (2002) cautioned that scenes actually fall on a continuum and mixed scenes are common.

What is a psychological autopsy? How is it conducted in equivocal death cases? The psychological autopsy (term coined in 1977 at the Los Angeles Medical Examiner's office, associated with Shneidman) is a retrospective reconstruction of a deceased person's state of mind, used in equivocal death analysis to help decide among the five manners of death: natural, accident, suicide, homicide or undetermined. It is conducted by interviewing family members, friends and associates, reviewing medical and personal records, examining the deceased's writings, habits, recent behaviour and stressors, and reconstructing the events and intentions preceding death — essentially producing a psychological profile of the deceased to determine whether the death was self-inflicted or otherwise.

How does Freud interpret dreams? Discuss dream interpretation in the Freudian model. For Freud, dreams are the 'royal road to the unconscious': they are disguised fulfilments of repressed wishes, mostly sexual in origin. Every dream symbol is ultimately a manifestation of sexual desires and of conflicts rooted in the psychosexual stages. The manifest content (the dream as remembered) hides the latent content (the true unconscious wish), transformed by dream-work processes such as condensation and displacement. The analyst uncovers the latent content through the patient's free association to the dream elements. Jung disagreed: he held that different symbols carry different, often archetypal and prospective meanings rather than uniformly sexual ones.

Discuss Jung's view of the unconscious. What, in Jung's account, is the underlying reason for human behaviour and violence? Jung divided the unconscious into the personal unconscious (repressed personal experiences and complexes) and the collective unconscious — an inherited, universal layer containing archetypes such as the Shadow, Anima, Animus, Hero, Great Mother, Trickster and Self. The underlying reason for behaviour, including violence, is the activity and imbalance of these archetypes and the ego's failure to integrate them: when the Shadow is dominant and unacknowledged, its aggression erupts in wars and brutality; when archetypes fail to work in a collimated (harmonious) manner, violence results. The goal of psychological life is individuation — realising the Self, which Jung compared with Iqbal's concept of Khudi.

Discuss the anal stage of psychosexual development. In what two ways do children meet the conflict of this stage? In Freud's model the anal stage (approximately 2–5 years in the handouts' sequence) centres on toilet training — the child's first experience of social control over a bodily pleasure. The conflict between the id's wish for immediate gratification and parental demands for control is met in two ways, producing two fixation patterns. (1) Anal retentive: the child holds on and resists; as an adult he becomes stingy, stubborn, obstinate and excessively orderly and clean. (2) Anal expulsive (explosive): the child rebels by soiling and defying control; as an adult he becomes messy, disorganised, rebellious, defiant and destructively careless. Both patterns reflect unresolved anal-stage conflict.

Discuss the Shadow archetype and its relationship with violence. The Shadow is the dark, hidden and repressed side of the personality — everything the person refuses to acknowledge in himself. Because the shadow is unconscious, the person projects his own evil onto others and remains blind to his own brutality. When the shadow becomes dominant, violence erupts on a large scale: nations go to war, violence epidemics and chaos appear, and even logical, masterminded leaders attack weaker countries and justify their cruelty while the whole world can see it but they cannot. The trickster's violence is similarly extreme. Integration of the shadow — recognising one's own capacity for evil — is therefore essential for controlling violence.

What is 'active imagination' in Jungian psychology? Active imagination is Jung's technique of consciously dialoguing with the unconscious. The patient focuses on an image, fantasy or figure arising from the unconscious and engages with it in waking dialogue, allowing the contents that lie immediately below the threshold of consciousness — those most likely to erupt spontaneously into the conscious mind — to be produced, expressed and understood. Unlike Freud's free association, which Jung found led away from the image, active imagination stays with the image and lets it develop, helping the patient integrate archetypal contents such as the shadow and move toward the Self.

What is modeling? Discuss Bandura's social learning explanation of aggression. Modeling is learning by observing and imitating a model — a live person or a symbolic model in media. Bandura argued that aggression is not inherited but learned through behaviour modeling: children who observe aggressive models (parents, peers, media heroes) acquire aggressive responses, especially when the model is reinforced — vicarious reinforcement. Four conditions are necessary for modeling: attention to the model, retention of the observed behaviour, motor reproduction (ability to perform it) and motivation. Similarity to the model, the model's prestige and the observability of the behaviour increase imitation. This is why children of aggressive, physically punishing parents tend to become bullies and aggressive adults.

Compare classical and operant conditioning. Classical conditioning (Pavlov) is S–R learning in which an association is formed between a neutral stimulus and an unconditioned stimulus, so that the now conditioned stimulus elicits the reflexive, involuntary response; no new behaviour is created, only a new trigger for an existing reflex, and the behaviour is elicited by antecedent stimuli. Operant conditioning (Skinner) concerns voluntary behaviour modified by its consequences: behaviours followed by reinforcement increase and those followed by punishment or non-reinforcement decrease (extinction). Skinner demonstrated it with rats pressing levers in the Skinner box for food pellets, and analysed how fixed and variable interval and ratio schedules of reinforcement control the rate of responding — the variable ratio schedule producing the highest rate.

'Punishment is not effective.' Discuss Skinner's position and its implications for violence. Skinner's experiments showed that mild punishment only temporarily suppresses behaviour, and that only consistent and intense punishment suppresses it completely — which is impractical and unethical with children. Punishment also generalises, suppressing desirable behaviour along with undesirable behaviour, and it can act as reinforcement when it gives the child the attention he wants. Its implications for violence are serious: physical punishment models aggression ('aggression begets aggression'), builds up rage, resentment and revenge fantasies, teaches the child to avoid the punisher rather than to behave well, and damages self-esteem; offenders frequently have childhood histories of physical punishment. Skinner's alternative is to reward desirable behaviour and ignore unwanted behaviour — energetic progress in good eliminates bad.

subjective.question: Discuss Foucault's model. What is its key concept? Michel Foucault's critical model holds that society has no tolerance for difference and seeks to create compliance. Its key concept is that institutions such as schools, prisons and mental hospitals are essentially similar machines of conformity: schools, like prisons, have fixed times announced by bells and fixed places for fixed tasks, and punish those who do not obey authority; mental hospitals serve the same normalising function as prisons. Foucault therefore regarded psychiatry and psychology as 'partners in crime' with the disciplinary system — partners in forcing different people into sameness rather than understanding or healing them.

subjective.topic: Humanistic and Other Models of Crime
subjective.question: Explain the bio-psycho-social model of crime. The bio-psycho-social model holds that biological predisposition, psychological factors and social/environmental factors all play equally important roles in making a person criminal. It accepts the genetic evidence (twin and adoption studies, e.g. Mednick et al., 1984, show a heritable basis for antisocial behaviour) but stresses parenting, attachment and cultural factors: genetic influence is stronger for early-onset antisocial behaviour, while later-onset delinquency is driven more by peer influence and lapses in parenting. The model is optimistic: it believes in treatment rather than punishment, argues that 'jails are factories of criminals' because new offenders are hardened by imprisonment, and proposes proportionate responses — punish the criminal, treat the mentally ill, and keep repeat offenders separate.

subjective.topic: Humanistic and Other Models of Crime
subjective.question: Discuss attachment theory's explanation of violence. Attachment theory proposes that the early affectional tie between child and caregiver determines later personality. Securely attached children — whose mothers respond promptly and consistently — learn to love and empathise. Early separation from mother or father, or physical abuse and maltreatment, is traumatic; trauma, especially in boys, produces numbing of emotions, suppression of empathy and compassion and flattening of feeling, which can result in cold-blooded violence. Case studies of violent offenders repeatedly show early separation and broken attachments. Avoidant attachment (little distress at departure, little response at return) and ambivalent attachment (inconsistent caregiving, preoccupation with the mother's availability) are the insecure patterns associated with later difficulties in relationships and self-control.

What is Tawba? Describe its stages. Tawba (repentance) is the basic process of the Islamic treatment of illnesses of the soul: the sinner feels regret and remorse, turns back to God and regains his essential purity through frequent self-renewal. Imam Ghazali's tradition describes its stages as: (1) feeling sincere remorse and regret for one's sins; (2) being frightened whenever one remembers past sins; (3) trying to eradicate injustice and support justice and right; (4) reviewing one's responsibilities and performing obligations previously neglected; (5) reforming oneself by removing the spiritual defects caused by deviation and error; and (6) regretting the times when one did not remember or thank God — remaining always apprehensive and alert so that thoughts and feelings are not tainted by anything that intervenes between oneself and God.

Describe the states of the Nafs and their parallels with Freud's model. The Qur'an describes states of the soul (Nafs). Nafs al-Ammara is the primitive soul that incites to evil, dominated by earthly desires (false pride, greed, jealousy, lust, backbiting, stinginess, malice); it closely resembles Freud's id. Nafs al-Lawwama is the self-blaming soul, conscious of its imperfections, blaming and reproaching itself after sin and repenting; it resembles the superego. Nafs al-Naatiqa distinguishes right from wrong through logic and reason and creates balance, paralleling the ego. Beyond Freud, Islam adds Nafs al-Mutma'inna — the soul at complete rest and peace, satisfied with the will of God — the final aim of perfection, which has no Freudian counterpart. The Islamic model of personality comprises three entities: Nafs, Qalb (heart) and Rooh (spirit).

List Imam Ghazali's treatments for the illnesses of the soul. Imam Ghazali, who also categorised the illnesses of the soul (lust, excessive hunger, idle talk and backbiting, anger, jealousy, love of the world, miserliness, love of power and fame, hypocrisy, pretension, pride and ignorance), prescribed these treatments: Tawba (repentance); Sabr o Shukr (patience/persistence and gratitude); Khauf o Rija (fear of Allah balanced with hope); Faqr o Zuhd (dependence on Allah and detachment from worldliness); Niyyat o Ikhlaas (pure intention and sincerity); Muhasiba o Muraqiba (self-accounting and meditation); Taffakkur (reflection on creation and one's purpose); Tawhid o Tawakkul (unity of Allah and trust in Him); Shauq o Muhabbat (longing and passionate love for Allah); and thinking about death and the Aakhirat (Hereafter).

What is antisocial personality disorder? Describe its main characteristics and the crimes typically committed by such individuals. Antisocial Personality Disorder (APD) — popularly called psychopathy — is a pervasive disregard for the rights of others and the rules of society. It can only be diagnosed after age 18, usually with a history of antisocial behaviour before 15 (lying, truancy, delinquency, running away). Main characteristics: typically male; absolute disregard for others' rights; manipulative, deceitful and conning; blaming others; pathological lying; poor impulse control; irresponsibility; sexual promiscuity; poly-drug use; thrill seeking; hostage taking; no victim empathy; and absolutely no remorse, regret or guilt. Such individuals typically commit theft, robbery, assault, rape, prison escape, illegal drug use and selling, sexual crimes and exploitation of vulnerable people — ranging from opportunistic mobile snatching to planned bank robbery. The DSPD debate asks whether such dangerous persons should be treated by force, given that psychiatry cannot predict dangerousness precisely and the disorder is considered largely untreatable against the person's will.

Discuss the developmental factors that produce a criminogenic personality. A criminogenic personality develops through the interaction of several factors: (1) personality traits that predispose the individual to criminality; (2) a biological basis for those traits; (3) early attachment failures such as maternal deprivation and lack of appropriate attachment; (4) socialisation patterns — friends, school environment and teachers; (5) early trauma, including removal from the home and childhood physical beatings and sexual abuse; (6) early separation from one or both parents and growing up without parental figures of both sexes; and (7) inconsistent parenting — one parent overindulgent and the other too strict, erratic discipline, absence of limit-setting and of a defined reward-and-punishment system — which teaches children to manipulate situations and exploit their parents' weaknesses.
